function.name: ask_user_question
function.description:
Present multiple-choice questions to the user and collect their answers.

Use this tool when you need the user to make a decision between several options, such as choosing
an implementation approach, selecting a library, or confirming a design choice.

Key constraints:
- 1-4 questions per call
- 2-4 options per question (an "Other" free-text option is always added automatically)
- Keep headers short (e.g. "Auth method", "Library"); headers over 16 characters are truncated
- Option labels should be 1-5 words

The user can:
- Select from the predefined options
- Type a custom answer via the "Other" option
- Skip or decline the question to ask for clarification

If the user submits answers, you will receive a key-value mapping of question text to their selections.
Questions the user skipped are marked with "skipped": true — treat a skipped question as the user
declining to choose, not as an error, and proceed with your best judgment.
If the user chooses to chat instead, you will receive a rejection with any partial answers they provided.

questions.description: Array of 1-4 question objects to present to the user.

question.description: The full question text to display to the user.

header.description:
Short label displayed as a chip/tag, e.g. "Auth method", "Library".
Labels longer than 16 characters are truncated with an ellipsis ("…") for display.

options.description: The choices presented to the user (2-4 options). An "Other" free-text option is always added automatically.

label.description: Display text the user sees (1-5 words).

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or its trade-offs.

multi_select.description: If true, the user can select multiple options; if false, single-select only.

answers.description:
User's answers, keyed by question text. Populated by the UI when the user responds.
Do not set this yourself; it will be filled in automatically.

additionalProperties.description: Represents a single answer from the user for one question.

selected.description:
The selected option label(s). For single-select, this will have one element.
For multi-select, it may have multiple. If "Other" was chosen, it will contain "Other".

custom_text.description: Custom text provided by the user. Set when the user selects "Other".

function.name: browser_preview
function.description:
Spin up a browser preview for a running web server.

This lets the USER interact with the web server as normal, and lets them send
you what they see: selecting a DOM element (with its React component and source
location, when resolvable) or the browser console output. Those captures go into
the USER's message box for them to send — you will not receive them unless they
do, so ask them to share what they see rather than waiting.

Usage notes:
  - The server must already be running; start it with a background command
    first (`timeout: 0`) if it isn't.
  - Returns immediately with a preview ID and URL. The preview stays up for the
    rest of the session, so the USER can keep using it after you stop.
  - An attempt is made to open the URL in the USER's browser; the URL is always
    printed in case that fails (e.g. over SSH or in a container).
  - Calling this again for the same URL returns the existing preview.
  - Use `close_browser_preview` when the preview is no longer needed, e.g.
    before shutting down the server it points at.

url.description:
The URL of the target web server to provide a browser preview for. This
should contain the scheme (e.g. http:// or https://), domain (e.g.
localhost or 127.0.0.1), and port (e.g. :8080) but no path.

name.description:
A short 3-5 word name for the target web server. Should be title-cased
e.g. 'Personal Website'. Format as a simple string, not as markdown; and
please output the title directly, do not prefix it with 'Title:' or
anything similar.

function.name: close_browser_preview
function.description:
Closes a running browser preview by its ID.

- Takes a preview_id parameter, as returned by `browser_preview`
- The preview URL stops working; the web server it points at is untouched
- Previews are closed automatically when the session ends, so this is only
  needed to close one early

preview_id.description: The ID of the browser preview to close.

function.name: edit
function.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must use your `read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file.
- When editing text from read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: spaces + line number + tab. Everything after that tab is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files to creating new ones.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replace_all` to change every instance of `old_string`.
- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

old_string.description: The text to replace. Always provide `old_string` before `new_string` so that streaming displays can show the diff progressively.

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from `old_string`)

function.name: exec
function.description:
Executes a given shell command in a persistent shell session and waits for output with optional timeout, ensuring proper handling and security measures.

Commands run under bash by default on every platform (Git Bash on Windows; PowerShell only if Git Bash is missing) unless you set `shell_flavor`. Write the command in that shell's syntax; never wrap it in another shell (`bash -lc "..."`, `powershell -Command "..."`), which parses your quoting and `$` expansions twice. To use a different shell, set `shell_flavor` (e.g. `shell_flavor: "powershell"` for Windows-native cmdlets).

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations like git, npm, docker, etc. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location
   - For example, before running "mkdir foo/bar", first use `ls foo` to check that "foo" exists and is the intended parent directory

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
   - Examples of proper quoting:
     - cd "/Users/name/My Documents" (correct)
     - cd /Users/name/My Documents (incorrect - will fail)
     - python "/path/with spaces/script.py" (correct)
     - python /path/with spaces/script.py (incorrect - will fail)
   - After ensuring proper quoting, execute the command.
   - Capture the output of the command.

Usage notes:
  - If the output is too long, it will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - Commands run in a persistent shell session for each shell_id, preserving state between calls. The working directory persists between commands.
  - One-shot commands (no `shell_id`) do NOT share state with each other: the working directory does NOT persist between calls. Use the optional `workdir` parameter (an absolute path to an existing directory) to set the working directory for a command, instead of a leading `cd` that the next call would forget. With a `shell_id`, `workdir` changes that session's directory before running the command.
  - Prefer one command per call: to do several things, make several calls in the same message instead of separating commands with `;` or a newline.
  - Chain with `&&` when a command must not run unless the previous one succeeded (PowerShell: `cmd1; if ($?) { cmd2 }`).
  - Use absolute paths in your commands instead of `cd` if possible. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it.
  - Passwords cannot be entered into this tool, so `sudo` fails when it needs one. Do NOT retry with a TTY or ask the user to type a password — run without sudo or ask the user to run the command themselves.

command.description:
The command to execute in the current shell session.

Examples:
- Bash: "echo 'Hello World'", "ls -la", "git status"
- PowerShell: "Write-Output 'Hello World'", "Get-ChildItem"

Note: Do NOT include the shell executable (like "bash -c" or "powershell -Command") in the command.
The command should be the raw shell command as you would type it in the active shell.

shell_id.description: Optional shell ID to reuse an existing interactive session. Use shell IDs to maintain multiple shell sessions. When shell ID is provided, writes to that session's stdin. When no shell ID is provided, a new session is created.

workdir.description: Optional absolute path to use as the working directory for this command (does not persist between one-shot calls; with a `shell_id` it cds the session).

timeout.description:
Optional timeout in milliseconds (default: background after 10s idle or 30s total).
When it elapses, a still-running command is backgrounded and its shell_id returned for `get_output`/`kill_shell`. Set to `0` to background immediately.

tty.description:
Allocate a PTY-backed interactive session. Default `false`.
`false` (default): one-shot non-interactive command run through pipes; good for most use cases.
`true`: persistent interactive session — for TUI programs (vim, tmux, top, REPLs) or state that must persist across calls.

shell_flavor.description:
Which shell runs the command: `bash`, `zsh`, `fish` or `powershell`.
Defaults to bash on every platform (Git Bash on Windows; PowerShell only
on a Windows machine without Git Bash). Pick a shell here instead of
nesting one shell inside another: the command is handed to it verbatim,
so `shell_flavor: "powershell"` runs plain PowerShell syntax with no
bash parse of your quoting and `$` expansions in between. Only valid
when starting a new shell: a `shell_id` that already exists keeps the
shell it was started with.

env.description:
Environment variables for this command's process tree, e.g.
`{"API_KEY": "abc123", "NODE_ENV": "development"}`. These take effect
only when a new shell is started, so `env` cannot be combined with
`shell_id` — omit `shell_id` (the call is rejected otherwise) so the
variables are set from the shell's first process onward. They are
visible to this command and its child processes only, not to other
shells or later commands.

function.name: find_file_by_name
function.description: Fast file name/path pattern matching tool that works with any codebase size using glob patterns. Supports brace expansion (e.g., `**/*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}`). Matches against file paths, not file contents. Do NOT use this tool for searching for things like function names, variable names, etc. which should be searched against file contents (e.g. using grep).

pattern.description:
The glob pattern to match files against.
Examples:
- `*.py` - matches all Python files in the current directory only (not subdirectories)
- `**/*.js` - matches all JavaScript files in the current directory and all subdirectories recursively
- `src/**/*.ts` - matches all TypeScript files within the `src` folder and its subdirectories
- `test_*.py` - matches Python files starting with `test_` in the current directory (e.g., `test_utils.py`)
- `**/*.{ts,tsx}` - matches all TypeScript files (both .ts and .tsx) recursively using brace expansion

path.description: The directory to search in (defaults to current working directory)

function.name: get_output
function.description:
Reads the output from a background shell process.

Usage notes:
- The shell_id argument is required (use the ID returned by the exec tool)
- You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 280000ms). Timeouts below 10000ms (10s) are raised to 10s; the default is 10s.
- IMPORTANT: timeout is the MAX wait — this returns immediately when the process exits. If you want to wait for a finite command to finish, set a long timeout and do not repeatedly poll. For a process that is expected to keep running (dev servers, watchers, daemons), a long timeout always waits the full duration — use a short timeout (10-30s) to read its startup output, repeating until the ready signal appears, or verify readiness directly (e.g. curl the port).
- The process continues running after reading output
- This will return the output of the most recently executed command in the shell if there is no current command running command

shell_id.description: The ID of the shell to read output from.

incremental.description:
If true (default), returns the changes since your last read. For interactive shells whose
screen redraws in place (progress bars, block redraws), this is a unified diff so in-place
line changes are shown as `-`old / `+`new; for plain append-only output it is the new lines.
If false, returns the full output buffer.

function.name: grep
function.description:
A powerful search tool built on ripgrep.

Usage:
- Always prefer this tool over invoking `grep` or `rg` as a shell command. It has been optimized for correct permissions and access.
- The pattern is treated as a regular expression using Rust regex syntax (like `rg` defaults): look-ahead/look-behind (e.g. `(?!...)`, `(?<=...)`) and backreferences are NOT supported. Rewrite without them, e.g. use `foo\([^)]` instead of `foo\((?!\))`.
- Filter files with the glob_pattern parameter in glob format (e.g., "*.rs", "src/**/*.py").
- Use output_mode to control results: 'content' for matching lines, 'files_with_matches' for file paths only, 'count' for match counts. Set case_insensitive for case-insensitive matching and context_lines to show lines around each match.
- If the result is truncated, narrow your search with a more specific pattern or more filters.
- Files larger than 4 MB are skipped.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for, passed to ripgrep under the hood

path.description: The directory or file to search in. Defaults to current directory.

glob_pattern.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g., '*.rs' searches .rs files in current dir but not subdirs, 'src/**/*.py' searches .py files in src/ and its subdirs). Defaults to searching all files.

case_insensitive.description: Perform case-insensitive search. Defaults to false.

max_results.description: Maximum number of matches to return. Defaults to 100, max 20,000. Only applicable for "content" output mode.

context_lines.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (context). Defaults to 0.

function.name: kill_shell
function.description:
Kills a running background shell by its ID.

- Takes a shell_id parameter identifying the shell to kill
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running shell

shell_id.description: The ID of the shell to kill.

function.name: mcp_call_tool
function.description: Execute a tool on an MCP server. Use this to interact with external services like Linear, GitHub, Slack, databases, and more. The tool result will be returned as structured data.

server_name.description: Name of the MCP server to use (e.g., "linear", "github").

tool_name.description: Name of the tool to execute.

arguments.description: Input arguments for the tool as a JSON object.

function.name: mcp_list_servers
function.description: Lists all MCP servers you have access to. Use this first if the user is asking about any third party integrations (e.g. Slack, Linear, etc).

function.name: mcp_list_tools
function.description: List available tools and resources from MCP servers. Use this to discover what capabilities are available before calling mcp_call_tool.

server_name.description: Name of the MCP server to list tools from (e.g., "linear", "github"). If not provided, lists tools from all configured servers.

function.name: mcp_read_resource
function.description: Read a resource from an MCP server. Resources can be files, database records, API responses, or any data exposed by the MCP server. Returns the resource content as text or binary data.

function.name: notebook_edit
function.description: Edit a cell in a Jupyter notebook file (.ipynb) - replace, insert, or delete cells

notebook_path.description: The absolute path to the Jupyter notebook file (.ipynb) to edit.

cell_number.description: The 0-based index of the cell to edit.

new_source.description: The new source content for the cell.

cell_type.description: The type of the cell. If not specified, keeps the current type (for replace) or defaults to code (for insert).

edit_mode.description: The edit operation to perform. Defaults to replace.

function.name: notebook_read
function.description: Read a Jupyter notebook file (.ipynb) and extract all cells with their outputs

notebook_path.description: The absolute path to the Jupyter notebook file to read (must be absolute, not relative)

function.name: read
function.description: Reads a file from the filesystem. The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path. By default, it reads up to 20000 characters starting from the beginning of the file. You can optionally specify a line offset and limit (especially handy for long files), but it's recommended to read the whole file by not providing these parameters. Any lines longer than 2000 characters will be truncated.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read.

offset.description: Optional line number to start reading from (1-based).

limit.description: Optional number of lines to read.

function.name: read_subagent
function.description: Reads the response from a background subagent, using the agent_id you got from the run_subagent tool or a <subagent_completion_notification> message. You use block=true to wait for completion. If you have other work to do, you can do that (you'll be notified whenever a subagent completes). This tool will never interrupt a running subagent.

agent_id.description: The ID of the background subagent to read output from.

block.description: If true, block until the subagent finishes or the timeout expires.

timeout.description: Maximum number of seconds to wait when blocking. Defaults to 30, capped at 600, unless the tool description documents different limits for a specific subagent type.

function.name: request_scope
function.description: Request read or write access to a directory. Use this tool when you encounter a permission error due to sandboxing and need access to a path outside your current allowed directories. The user will be prompted to approve or deny the request. This tool is a no-op if the scope is already granted.

scope.description: The type of access to request: "read" or "write".

path.description: The absolute path to the directory to request access to.

function.name: run_subagent
function.description:
Launch an independent subagent to handle a task autonomously.

Subagents (also referred to as just "agents") handle self-contained, multi-step tasks, such as broad or uncertain searches. When you do run several at once, launch them in parallel rather than one after the other, and keep their work disjoint so they don't interfere with each other (e.g. no two subagents writing the same files).

Skip subagents when simpler tools suffice:
- If you already know the file path, read it directly
- Use your grep and glob tools rather than subagents when you think they will meet your needs quickly without many attempts
- Use your edit or read tools directly if only a few files are involved

- Don't use a subagent to do singular tasks like running a command

Writing effective prompts:
- Subagents are stateless; they cannot ask clarifying questions, and they can't see any of your context. Front-load all context they might neeed: relevant file paths, function/class names, what you already know, and exactly what you need back.
- State whether the subagent should make changes or only investigate. It has no visibility into the user's original request. When asking open-ended questions, explicitly state how thorough of an answer you want.
Usage notes:
- The user never sees subagent output directly, so you'll need to distill subagents' answers into your own response if you want to .
- You can generally trust subagent results. Avoid re-doing their work unless something looks wrong.

- Set is_background=true to run a background subagent without blocking. You will be notified automatically when it finishes with a <subagent_completion_notification> message. You can check on the status of a background subagent using your read_subagent tool. To wait for a subagent to complete to see its response, call read_subagent with block=true. Background agents are nice for parallelism and work that might take unexpectedly long, in which case you'd want to do other work while waiting.
        - Set is_background=false to run a foreground subagent when you need the answer before continuing. You can't do any other work while a foreground subagent is running, and at most one foreground agent can run at once. Despite these restrictions, foreground users have a slightly nicer UX and are less frequently blocked by permission issues. So use is_background=false when you don't need paralellism and would have otherwise spawned a background agent then immediately called read_subagent with block=true.
        - If you want to run both background subagents and a foreground subagent, run the background subagents first and then run the foreground subagent. Don't try to launch multiple foreground subagents in parallel; instead use background subagents or run the foreground subagents sequentially so you can see each subagent's output before launching the next one.

title.description: A short, human-readable title for this subagent.

task.description: The task or prompt to give the subagent. Be specific and detailed.

profile.description: The id of the profile to use for this subagent.

is_background.description:
If true, the subagent runs in the background and returns its ID
immediately. You will be automatically woken up with the result
when it completes. You can check progress with read_subagent if
needed, but do not poll in a loop — just continue with other work
or end your turn.

resume.description:
If set to an agent id (which you can get from the response of a previous
run_subagent invocation), your prompt will be sent to that agent, so it can
respond using its existing execution transcript as context.

function.name: skill
function.description: Invoke or discover skills. Modes: 'invoke' (default) activates a skill by name; 'list' and 'search' accept exactly one source, either a project `path` or `source: "plugins"` for active plugin skills. 'list' scans only the project root; 'search' recurses and filters by optional keywords. Use plugin search before concluding that a referenced plugin skill does not exist.

command.description: The skill operation to perform. Defaults to "invoke" if omitted.

skill.description:
The name of the skill to invoke (required for 'invoke' command).
Use one of the available skills listed in the system prompt.

path.description:
Project path to discover skills in. Scans skill directories (e.g.
.devin/skills/) at the project root; `list` does not recurse into
subdirectories, while `search` does. Relative paths are resolved
against the session's working directory. Provide either `path` or
`source` for list/search, not both.

source.description:
Set to `plugins` to list or search active plugin skills instead of
scanning a project path.

keywords.description: List of keywords to search for. Empty or omitted means include all skills.

keywords_mode.description: Controls whether all keywords or any keyword need to be present.

function.name: todo_write
function.description:
Use this tool to create and manage a structured task list for your current session. It tracks your progress and gives the user visibility into what you are working on.

## When to use
Use this tool for multi-step tasks (3 or more distinct steps), non-trivial tasks that require planning, or when the user provides multiple tasks or explicitly asks for a todo list. Skip it for trivial, single-step, or purely conversational/informational requests — just do the task directly.

## Task states and management
- Each task is pending, in_progress, or completed
- Keep exactly ONE task in_progress at a time; mark it in_progress when starting work on it
- Mark a task completed IMMEDIATELY after finishing it
- Only mark a task completed when it is fully done — if you hit errors or blockers, keep it in_progress and add a new task describing what must be resolved
- Add follow-up tasks discovered during work; remove tasks that are no longer relevant
- Create specific, actionable items and break complex work into smaller steps

## Example
For "Add a dark mode toggle to settings, then run tests and build":
1. Add dark mode toggle component to settings page (in_progress)
2. Wire up dark mode state management
3. Update existing components to support theme switching
4. Run tests and build, fixing any failures

todos.description: The updated list of todo items.

status.description: Current status of the todo item.

function.name: web_search
function.description:
Search the web for information using a search query. Returns relevant web page titles, URLs, and summaries. Use this when you need to find information online.

You must not include extraneous information in web searches. For example, to find latest python version, do *NOT* search "latest Python version 2026 3.11 3.12 3.13". The "2026 3.11 3.12 3.13" is unnecessary. Keep the search string simple and focused, e.g. "latest Python version".

query.description: The search query to find relevant web pages.

num_results.description: Maximum number of results to return. Defaults to 5.

domain.description: Optional domain to restrict search results to (e.g. "docs.rs").

function.name: webfetch
function.description: Fetches a web page and returns its content as readable text.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from.

function.name: write
function.description:
Write content to a file, creating it if needed and overwriting it if it exists.

Usage:
- Prefer the edit tool for modifying existing files. Only use this tool to create new files or for complete rewrites.
- If overwriting an existing file, you SHOULD use the read tool first to read the file's contents.
- NEVER proactively create documentation files (*.md) or README files unless explicitly requested.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid writing emojis to files unless asked.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write

content.description: The content to write to the file

function.name: write_to_process
function.description:
Writes input to an interactive process running in a shell with support for both text and special characters.

IMPORTANT: This command will NOT work if there is no command running in the shell. If you want to execute a command in the shell use the exec tool.

Provide exactly ONE of text_input or bytes_input (never both). To answer a prompt that needs an Enter keypress (e.g. a [y/n] prompt), set bytes_input to y<CR> (the y character followed by Enter).

Input options:
- text_input: Literal text content (no special character interpretation)
- bytes_input: Special characters using angle bracket notation (e.g., <ESC>, <CR>, <UP>, <C-c>)

Special character notation:
- <ESC> = Escape character
- <CR> = Carriage return (Enter)
- <LF> = Line feed (newline)
- <BS> = Backspace
- <UP>, <DOWN>, <LEFT>, <RIGHT> = Arrow keys
- <C-c>, <C-d>, <C-z> = Ctrl+key combinations

shell_id.description: The ID of the shell to write to.

text_input.description: Text content to write to the shell (interpreted as literal text).

bytes_input.description: Special characters/bytes to write to the shell (interpreted with angle bracket notation).

steps.message:
You are Devin, an interactive command line agent from Cognition.

Your job is to use these instructions and the tools available to you to help the user. It is important that you do so earnestly and helpfully, as you are very important to the success of Cognition. Best of luck! We love you. <3

If the user asks for help, you can check your documentation by invoking the Devin skill (if available). Otherwise, this information may be helpful:

- /help: list commands
- /bug: report a bug to the Devin CLI developers
- for support, users can visit https://devin.ai/support

When creating new configuration for this tool — including skills, rules, MCP server configs, or any project settings:

- Always use the `.devin/` directory for NEW configuration (e.g. `.devin/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `.devin/config.json`)
- For global (user-level) configuration, use `~/.config/devin/`
- Do NOT place new configuration in `.claude/`, `.cursor/`, or other tool-specific directories unless explicitly asked. These are only read for compatibility, not written to.
- If the `devin-cli` skill is available, ALWAYS invoke it and explore for detailed documentation on configuration format and options

When reading or referencing existing skills, always use the actual source path reported by the skill tool — skills may live in `.devin/`, `.agents/`, or other directories.


# Modes

The active mode is how the user would like you to act.

- Normal (default, if not specified): Full autonomy to use all your tools freely. For example: exploring a codebase, writing or editing code, etc.
- Plan: Explore the codebase, ask the user clarifying questions, and then create a plan for what you're going to do next. Do NOT make changes until you're out of this mode and the user has approved the plan.

Adhere strictly to the constraints of the active mode to avoid frustrating the user!


# Style

## Professional Objectivity

Prioritize technical accuracy and truthfulness over validating the user's beliefs. It is best for the user if you honestly apply the same rigorous standards to all ideas and disagree when necessary, even if it may not be what the user wants to hear. Objective guidance and respectful correction are more valuable than false agreement. Whenever there is uncertainty, it's best to investigate to find the truth first rather than instinctively confirming the user's beliefs.

## Tone

- Be concise, direct, and to the point. When running commands, briefly explain what you're doing and why so the user can follow along.
- Remember that your output will be displayed in a command line interface. Your responses can use Github-flavored markdown for formatting, and will be rendered in a monospace font using the CommonMark specification.
- Output text to communicate with the user; all text you output outside of tool use is displayed to the user. Only use tools to complete tasks. Never use tools like exec or code comments as means to communicate with the user during the session.
- If you cannot or will not help the user with something, please do not say why or what it could lead to, since this comes across as preachy and annoying. Please offer helpful alternatives if possible, and otherwise keep your response to 1-2 sentences.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid using emojis in all communication unless asked.
- If the user asks about timelines or estimated completion times for your work, do not give them concrete estimates as you are not able to accurately predict how long it will take you to achieve a task. Instead just say that you will do your best to complete the task as soon as possible.
- Avoid guessing. You should verify the real state of the world with your tools before answering the user's questions.

<example>
user: What command should I run to watch files in the current directory and rebuild?

  1|# From Layered Design to Agent-Guided Hardware–Program Co-design
  2|
  3|## Why this assignment exists
  4|
  5|Modern AI infrastructure is built as a stack. A model defines the computation. A compiler chooses kernels, tiling, data movement, and instruction order. A runtime schedules work. A hardware architect chooses compute units, memory capacity, bandwidth, and interconnect.
  6|
  7|These layers are useful, but they are not independent. A larger matrix engine helps only if the program can supply enough work and data. More on-chip memory helps only if the compiler finds reuse that avoids expensive off-chip accesses. A schedule that is efficient on one accelerator may perform poorly on another.
  8|
  9|In principle, we could describe all of these choices in one optimization problem. In practice, the joint search space is enormous. Hardware choices multiply with program choices, and program behavior depends on the hardware on which it runs. Traditional system design therefore separates the problem into layers and relies heavily on abstractions, heuristics, and human experience. This is not a conceptual failure. It is a practical response to a problem that has been too large and uncertain to search as a whole.
 10|
 11|This assignment asks whether that boundary can now move.
 12|
 13|## Why AI inference changes the problem
 14|
 15|General-purpose programs often contain input-dependent branches, irregular memory access, unpredictable synchronization, and rapidly changing workloads. These behaviors make it difficult to predict how a program will use a proposed machine before the program actually runs.
 16|
 17|Transformer inference is different in several important ways. For a fixed model and deployment scenario:
 18|
 19|- the operator graph is largely known;
 20|- tensor shapes and dependencies are explicit;
 21|- the same layer structure is executed repeatedly;
 22|- data movement and storage requirements can be modeled;
 23|- important deployment cases, such as prompt prefill and token-by-token decoding, can be specified precisely.
 24|
 25|Inference is not perfectly static. Sequence lengths vary, memory contention matters, and prefill and decode expose very different kinds of parallelism. Nevertheless, the workload is regular enough that a simulator can evaluate many hardware–program pairs under a common model of correctness, latency, area, power, and energy.
 26|
 27|This regularity does not make co-design easy. It makes a larger part of the problem explicit and measurable.
 28|
 29|## What agent-guided optimization adds
 30|
 31|Even for a fixed Transformer, exhaustively enumerating every legal accelerator and every legal program remains impractical. The opportunity is therefore not to replace the entire design process with one monolithic solver. It is to search selectively.
 32|
 33|An AI agent can maintain a history of proposed designs and their measured outcomes. It can use that evidence to generate new candidates, reject invalid or unpromising regions, and decide which experiments are most informative. Mathematical optimization methods, including mixed-integer linear programming when appropriate, can solve bounded subproblems or enforce exact constraints. A compiler or program generator can turn each software candidate into executable assembly. A deterministic simulator can then provide the feedback needed to revise both the hardware and the program.

 35|The resulting loop is:

 41|5. **Measure the design.** Estimate latency, area, power, energy, and other relevant costs.
 42|6. **Learn from the result.** Use the evidence to refine the search and propose the next candidate.
 43|
 44|The agent does not remove the combinatorial search problem, and the simulator does not guarantee that the best observed design is globally optimal. Together, however, they make it possible to explore across boundaries that a conventional layer-by-layer process would normally hold fixed.

  1|# Complete assembly reference
  2|
  3|This is the public instruction set for the frozen two-case challenge. For the structure of the two complete Transformer programs, see the [assembly walkthrough](/assembly-guide/) and the [P1](/examples/M1_P1.asm) and [D1](/examples/M2_D1.asm) listings. Every nonempty line has the form `OPCODE {"field": ...}`. A line beginning with `#` is a comment. JSON objects must have unique keys and finite numeric values; unknown opcodes and malformed loop bodies are rejected, including bodies of zero-trip loops. Programs are FP32, have no data-dependent branch, and may use at most 8 MiB of source text, 32 nested static loops, and 10 million expanded instructions per case.
  4|
  5|**Source of truth:** the starter ZIP contains the exact parser (`codesign/challenge/isa.py`), functional executor (`micro.py`), race checker (`hbm_race.py`), timing scheduler (`pipeline_events.py`), HBM layout (`abi.py`), and local command line checker (`challenge.py`). This page states the complete authoring contract; use those files when checking a corner case. `OPCODE` and JSON must be on the **same physical line**. Blank lines and whole-line `#` comments are accepted. Inline comments, labels, registers named in free-form text, branches, and opcodes outside the table below are not accepted. Operand keys and opcode spellings are case-sensitive. Except for the documented legacy sync shorthand, use exactly the listed top-level fields.
  6|
  7|## Operand format
  8|
  9|A memory view is a JSON object such as:
 10|
 11|```json
 12|{"space":"RF","offset":0,"count":48,"wg":"g0","lane":0}
 13|```
 14|
 15|| Field | Meaning |
 16|| --- | --- |
 17|| `space` | `HBM`, `SH`, or `RF` |
 18|| `offset` | Starting FP32 **element** offset within the selected space |
 19|| `count` | Number of logical FP32 elements, positive |
 20|| `wg` | Workgroup name for RF/SH; `null` for HBM |
 21|| `lane` | RF storage partition number; 0 for HBM/SH |
 22|| `shape` (optional) | One- or two-dimensional positive logical extents |
 23|| `strides` (optional) | Matching positive element strides; `count` equals the product of `shape` |
 24|
 25|All five base fields are required, even for HBM. `HBM` uses `"wg":null,"lane":0`; `SH` uses the active workgroup's name and lane 0; `RF` uses the active workgroup's name and a lane index. `offset` and `count` are nonnegative/positive **integers**, not byte addresses or booleans. Every word is four bytes. The actual address of a shaped view is `offset + i*strides[0]` for one dimension, or `offset + i*strides[0] + j*strides[1]` for two; the element order is row-major over the logical indices. The largest touched offset must fit the space. For a contiguous view, omit both optional fields. For a one-dimensional strided view, specify `"shape":[count],"strides":[stride]`; for a matrix tile, specify both two-element arrays. A destination view must not touch the same physical location twice.
 26|
 27|Without `shape`/`strides`, the view is contiguous. For a two-dimensional tile, supply **both** arrays: `count` is the product of `shape`, while `strides` gives the physical element increments in the source space. A write view cannot visit the same element twice. HBM offsets come from the public [ABI list](/abi/) and have a 2 GiB boundary. RF is private to one workgroup and partition; SH is private to one workgroup. A workgroup's RF slot is 64 KiB, divided among the RF partitions selected by the hardware vector width. SH accesses must stay within its declared byte quota. No instruction may read unwritten RF/SH data, cross into another workgroup's RF/SH, write a read-only HBM symbol, or read a future step's input. The [assembly walkthrough](/assembly-guide/#4-read-hbm-operands-as-element-addresses) works through a real strided weight tile.
 28|
 29|For RF, `lane` ranges from 0 through `vector_lanes - 1`; each partition has `65536 / (4 * vector_lanes)` FP32 elements. RF offsets are **within a partition**, so lane 1 offset 0 is a different word from lane 0 offset 0. SH has `shared_bytes / 4` words per workgroup. HBM is a flat `2 GiB / 4`-word space; consult the [public ABI](/abi/) for named ranges. Scratch and required outputs begin invalid and need a write before a read. Required output/KV positions cannot be written twice; weights, original inputs, and history are read-only. A transfer or compute may overwrite its own input only when the operation's read has completed; the scheduler checks pending hazards.
 30|
 31|An `event` is a unique nonempty name for an operation. Loop-index interpolation such as `"load_{i}"` is allowed after a `FOR` binds `i`.
 32|
 33|**Operand helpers for generators:** a transfer's `src` and `dst` are full memory views. `MMA.ACC` uses three RF views named `a`, `b`, `acc`. `REDUCE` and `SFU` use RF `src` and `dst`. `VEC.src` is an array of RF views or immediate objects of the exact form `{"imm":number}`; `VEC.dst` is an RF view. There is no implicit HBM-to-compute path: load into RF first. A destination is initialized by a prior operation unless the instruction overwrites every destination element without reading it; `MMA.ACC` specifically **reads and updates** `acc`.
 34|
 35|## Complete opcode list
 36|
 37|| Opcode | Required JSON fields | Effect |
 38|| --- | --- | --- |
 39|| `WG.BEGIN` | `wg`, `sm`, `shared_bytes` | Start a named workgroup on a target SM and reserve a private RF slot and SH quota. Quota is a nonnegative multiple of four bytes. |
 40|| `WG.END` | `wg` | End a workgroup and release its RF/SH contents and residency. |
 41|| `LD` | `src`, `dst`, `event` | Copy an equal-size view between different spaces. HBM↔RF, HBM↔SH, and SH↔RF are allowed. |
 42|| `ST` | `src`, `dst`, `event` | The same explicit transfer semantics as `LD`; commonly used for writes to HBM. |
 43|| `MMA.ACC` | `a`, `b`, `acc`, `m`, `n`, `k`, `event` | Accumulate an `m×k` RF matrix times a `k×n` RF matrix into an `m×n` RF accumulator. Requires TC > 0. |
 44|| `VEC` | `kind`, `src`, `dst`, `event` | Elementwise RF operation. `src` is a list of RF views or finite FP32 immediates. |
 45|| `REDUCE` | `kind`, `src`, `dst`, `event` | Reduce one RF vector with `sum` or `max` to a one-element RF destination. |
 46|| `SFU` | `kind`, `src`, `dst`, `event` | Apply `exp`, `rsqrt`, or `tanh` elementwise to an RF vector. |
 47|| `WAIT` | `wg`, `events` | Make one active workgroup wait for named earlier events. |
 48|| `BARRIER` | `wgs`, `events` | Synchronize the listed active workgroups and named earlier events. |
 49|| `STEP.COMMIT` | `step` | Global step barrier, with zero-based consecutive step numbers. Wait for preceding work and check output/KV coverage before releasing the next external input. |
 50|| `FOR` | `var`, `start`, `stop`, `step` | Start a static half-open integer loop; `step` is positive. |
 51|| `END.FOR` | no fields (`{}`) | End the matching loop. |
 52|
 53|### Exact instruction behavior
 54|
 55|- **`WG.BEGIN {"wg":string,"sm":int,"shared_bytes":int}`**: `wg` is nonempty and not already active. `sm` is in `[0, sm_count)`. `shared_bytes` is a nonnegative multiple of 4, no larger than that SM's total shared-memory capacity. It creates fresh private RF/SH validity state. At most four workgroups can be physically resident on an SM, and concurrent resident SH quotas must fit; more logical groups may wait in the timing scheduler. **`WG.END {"wg":string}`** closes an active group, waits for its pending transfers, and permits later reuse of the name with fresh storage. Every group must end before program completion.
 56|- **`LD` and `ST`** each take exactly `{"src":view,"dst":view,"event":string}`. They perform the same elementwise copy of equal positive logical counts between **different** spaces: HBM↔RF, HBM↔SH, or SH↔RF. `ST` is conventionally used when writing HBM, but its opcode does not impose direction. RF↔SH requires the same workgroup in both views. Cross-workgroup RF/SH copies and transfers within one space are invalid. The two views may have different shapes/strides if their flattened logical element counts agree; values copy in logical order. An event identifies this transfer for later synchronization.
 57|- **`MMA.ACC {"a":view,"b":view,"acc":view,"m":int,"n":int,"k":int,"event":string}`**: `m,n,k` are positive. All three views are RF in the same workgroup, possibly in different lanes. Flattened `a`, `b`, and `acc` counts must be `m*k`, `k*n`, and `m*n`. Reshape them row-major and compute `acc += a @ b`, writing the accumulator back in place. TC count must be nonzero. Initialize `acc`, commonly with `VEC add` of two zero immediates, before the first MMA. Instruction tile dimensions need not equal physical TC dimensions; the service model charges hardware tile tails.
 58|- **`VEC {"kind":string,"src":[...],"dst":view,"event":string}`**: all memory operands are RF in the same workgroup. Each RF source has either one value, broadcast to every destination element, or exactly the destination count. Immediates broadcast after conversion to finite FP32. Source order and exact arity are defined in the vector table below. Destination must have a positive count; results must be finite when written.
 59|- **`REDUCE {"kind":"sum"|"max","src":view,"dst":view,"event":string}`**: RF source and RF destination belong to the same workgroup; source count is positive and destination count must be **one**. `sum` uses a neighboring-pair FP32 binary tree, carrying an odd final item to the next level. `max` takes the maximum. The single result must be finite.
 60|- **`SFU {"kind":"exp"|"rsqrt"|"tanh","src":view,"dst":view,"event":string}`**: RF source/destination in one workgroup with **equal counts**. The operations are elementwise `exp(x)`, `1/sqrt(x)`, and `tanh(x)`. Invalid domains, overflow, and any nonfinite result fail when written. Hardware `sfu_lanes` affects service time, not the functional formula.
 61|- **`WAIT {"wg":string,"events":[string,...]}`**: the target must be active. Every event name must have been produced earlier in the expanded instruction stream, and names in the list must be unique. The target waits for those event completions. An empty events list is allowed and adds no event dependency.
 62|- **`BARRIER {"wgs":[string,...],"events":[string,...]}`**: `wgs` is a nonempty, duplicate-free list of active groups; `events` follows the same rules as `WAIT`. Listed groups meet at the same barrier and wait for preceding work in its scope; unlisted groups are not participants. Use this to establish cross-group ordering when needed.
 63|- **`STEP.COMMIT {"step":int}`**: steps start at 0 and must be consecutive. It globally waits for previous work and outstanding transfers, checks every required hidden/KV output for that step, and releases the next external input. P1 needs commit 0 after both 64-position prompts and before its first new input; the final new position is checked at case end. D1 needs commits 0–7, one after each decode output. A commit may occur after all workgroups end.
 64|
 65|The legacy `WAIT {"events":[...]}` or `BARRIER {"events":[...]}` form is accepted only when exactly one workgroup is active. Explicit `wg`/`wgs` is recommended. A waited event must already be defined in source order. A workgroup preserves its own program order. Source-text interleaving alone does not order overlapping HBM reads/writes across workgroups; use a matching `WAIT`, a `BARRIER` covering the groups, or a cross-step `STEP.COMMIT`.
 66|
 67|`WG.BEGIN` can create more logical active groups than the SM can run simultaneously; the timing engine queues them. At most four are physically resident per SM, and their declared SH quotas must fit. `WG.END` is required before the name can be reused. `STEP.COMMIT` also works when no group remains active.
 68|
 69|## Vector kinds and operand counts
 70|
 71|| `VEC kind` | Sources | Result |
 72|| --- | ---: | --- |
 73|| `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div` | 2 | Corresponding FP32 arithmetic |
 74|| `fma` | 3 | `a*b+c`, rounded to FP32 at the instruction boundary |
 75|| `gt` | 2 | 1.0 where `a>b`, otherwise 0.0 |
 76|| `select` | 3 | Choose second source where first is nonzero, otherwise third |
 77|| `max` | 2 | Elementwise maximum |
 78|
 79|A source RF view may have one element (broadcast) or the destination count. An immediate is `{"imm": 1.0}` and must round to finite FP32. `VEC`, `SFU`, `REDUCE`, and `MMA.ACC` may read different RF partitions of the **same** workgroup. `REDUCE` has a one-element destination. `MMA.ACC` sizes must be `m*k`, `k*n`, and `m*n`, respectively; the three matrices are row-major.
 80|
 81|Vector source order is semantic: `sub` computes source 0 minus source 1, `div` divides source 0 by source 1, `fma` computes source 0 × source 1 + source 2, and `select` tests source 0 then picks source 1 or 2. `gt` uses a strict comparison. The executor rounds written values to FP32; `fma` forms its multiply-add in float64 before that FP32 write. Do not assume an arbitrary sequence of `VEC` instructions is bitwise equal to a fused `fma`. `div` by zero, `exp` overflow, and `rsqrt` of a negative value fail through the finite-write rule. Even if all values are finite, the scored outputs must also satisfy the reference tolerances in the [statement](/statement/#1-the-challenge).
 82|
 83|`MMA.ACC` groups consecutive K terms by hardware `tc_k_parallel`. Each group uses a fixed neighboring binary reduction tree, then groups accumulate in ascending K order. A tail group is zero-filled. Ordinary `REDUCE sum` also uses a fixed binary tree. Each instruction rounds its output to FP32. Physical TC tail slots still cost time and energy; shorter views mask only out-of-range memory accesses.
 84|
 85|## Static loops and expressions
 86|
 87|A loop uses compiled integer bounds, for example:
 88|
 89|```asm
 90|FOR {"var":"i","start":0,"stop":3,"step":1}
 91|VEC {"kind":"add","src":[{"space":"RF","offset":{"index":"i","scale":4,"offset":0},"count":4,"wg":"g","lane":0},{"imm":1.0}],"dst":{"space":"RF","offset":{"index":"i","scale":4,"offset":0},"count":4,"wg":"g","lane":0},"event":"add_{i}"}
 92|END.FOR {}
 93|```
 94|
 95|An integer operand may use `{"var":"i"}`, the affine form `{"index":"i","scale":4,"offset":0}`, or `{"add":[...]}`, `{"mul":[...]}`, `{"min":[...]}`, `{"max":[...]}`, `{"mod":[a,b]}`, and `{"ceildiv":[a,b]}`. Expressions resolve from static loop indices. There is no runtime data-dependent branch or unbounded loop.
 96|
 97|`FOR` has exactly `var`, `start`, `stop`, and `step`. The variable must be an identifier and cannot duplicate an enclosing loop variable. Bound values become nonnegative integers after substitution, `stop >= start`, and `step >= 1`. Iterations are `start, start + step, ...` strictly less than `stop`. An `END.FOR {}` closes one matching `FOR`. Every loop body is parsed even when its trip count is zero. Static integer expressions can be nested and can contain **negative integer constants inside arithmetic**, such as `{"mul":[-1,{"var":"k"}]}` for a tail calculation; the final operand must still satisfy its own range. `add`, `mul`, `min`, and `max` require at least two integer arguments; `mod` and `ceildiv` require exactly two with a positive divisor. Affine `scale` and `offset` must each be nonnegative integers. The same expressions can appear inside numeric fields of instructions and nested loop bounds. Strings containing braces interpolate a bound loop index, e.g. `"load_{i}"`; format specifications and conversions are unsupported. Give every expanded **event-bearing operation** a distinct event, including across loop iterations and reused workgroup names.
 98|
 99|### Ordering and timing rules
100|
101|The functional executor walks expanded instructions in source order to check values, but the performance model places workgroup instructions on separate streams. Program order is preserved **within** each workgroup. The text order of instructions from two different workgroups does not establish ordering for overlapping HBM reads and writes. The race checker rejects an unordered cross-group read/write or write/write overlap. To communicate through HBM, have the consumer wait on the producer's earlier event, place both groups in a barrier, or cross a `STEP.COMMIT` boundary. A `WAIT` event can be produced by another workgroup. `WAIT` does not automatically join all groups; `BARRIER` applies to exactly the listed groups. A commit is global.
102|
103|Transfers have latency and may remain pending after issue. If a later operation uses data produced by a transfer, or overwrites a transfer's RF/SH source while a store is still reading it, the timed checker imposes the dependency; use explicit event waits when expressing cross-group intent. Local RF/SH and HBM resource service, DMA queues, TC/vector/SFU/reduction units, cache, NoC, and HBM all influence the score. The [public scheduler](/model/pipeline_events.py) and [service formulas](/model/service.py) define those timings. The functional ISA alone does not promise one cycle per instruction or unlimited parallelism.
104|
105|### Before emitting a complete program
106|
107|1. Read the [HBM ABI](/abi/) for each case's tensor base, shape, read-only status, output range, and step-release rule. P1 and D1 are distinct programs with distinct layouts. Hardware JSON is shared.
108|2. Allocate only legal RF lanes, RF offsets, and SH quotas for that hardware. Initialize accumulators and scratch before reading them. Use shaped views for noncontiguous matrix tiles; `count` is the logical element count, not the physical span.
109|3. Produce every required final hidden and new K/V value exactly once; commit P1 prompt and D1 steps at the required boundaries. End every workgroup and ensure event names stay unique after expansion.
110|4. Run the starter package's `python challenge.py check --hardware hardware.json --program-p1 programs/M1_P1.asm --program-d1 programs/M2_D1.asm --seed 7 --report check.json` before running `estimate` or `grade`. See [the full development workflow](/assembly-guide/#7-generate-check-and-submit). The [complete P1](/examples/M1_P1.asm) and [D1](/examples/M2_D1.asm) listings provide executable patterns for every instruction used by the baseline.
111|
112|## Small worked instruction sequence
113|
114|For HBM values `[1,2,3,4,5,6,0,0]`, this program computes `1×4+2×5+3×6=32` into HBM element 7. This is an ISA illustration; full scored submissions must compute both complete Transformer cases.
115|
116|```asm
117|WG.BEGIN {"wg":"g","sm":0,"shared_bytes":0}
118|LD {"src":{"space":"HBM","offset":0,"count":3,"wg":null,"lane":0},"dst":{"space":"RF","offset":0,"count":3,"wg":"g","lane":0},"event":"a"}
119|LD {"src":{"space":"HBM","offset":3,"count":3,"wg":null,"lane":0},"dst":{"space":"RF","offset":3,"count":3,"wg":"g","lane":0},"event":"b"}
120|LD {"src":{"space":"HBM","offset":6,"count":1,"wg":null,"lane":0},"dst":{"space":"RF","offset":6,"count":1,"wg":"g","lane":0},"event":"z"}
121|MMA.ACC {"a":{"space":"RF","offset":0,"count":3,"wg":"g","lane":0},"b":{"space":"RF","offset":3,"count":3,"wg":"g","lane":0},"acc":{"space":"RF","offset":6,"count":1,"wg":"g","lane":0},"m":1,"n":1,"k":3,"event":"mma"}
122|WAIT {"wg":"g","events":["mma"]}
123|ST {"src":{"space":"RF","offset":6,"count":1,"wg":"g","lane":0},"dst":{"space":"HBM","offset":7,"count":1,"wg":null,"lane":0},"event":"out"}
124|WG.END {"wg":"g"}
125|```
126|
127|A write from RF or SH may continue reading its source after the `ST` is issued. Overwriting an overlapping source must wait until that read service finishes. All live groups must eventually end, every required step must commit, and every required output/KV word must be written. P1's required commit is after the prompt; D1 commits all eight decode steps. The complete baseline P1 and D1 assembly listings are available as [individual downloads](/examples/M1_P1.asm) and [the starter ZIP](/downloads/transformer-codesign-starter.zip).

读完了。这是一个 **Transformer 推理的硬件–程序协同设计作业（starter包）**，核心任务和结构如下：

## 任务本质

提交一个 ZIP：`hardware.json`（一份共享的加速器配置）+ `programs/M1_P1.asm` + `programs/M2_D1.asm` + 过程记录。目标是在保证数值正确的前提下最小化模拟周期数。

- **M1_P1**：3层、宽256、8头×32、FFN 1024 的模型；batch=2，各算64位 prompt 的 prefill，`STEP.COMMIT {"step":0}` 后再各算1个新位置（共130个 hidden + 每层 KV）。
- **M2_D1**：2层、宽128、4头×32、FFN 512 的小模型；已有128位历史 KV 在 HBM，顺序 decode 8 步，每步都要 `STEP.COMMIT`。

**评分**：`score = 1000 × sqrt((30996995/T_P1) × (1302032/T_D1))`，基线=1000。门槛：两 case 都正确（容差 `1e-3+1e-3·|ref|`）、面积 ≤24mm²、峰值滚动功耗 ≤20W、各 case ≤2×基线周期。时钟固定 500MHz。

## 关键文件

| 文件 | 作用 |
|---|---|
| `hardware.json` | 当前基线配置：8 SM、2 TC(4x8,k=1)、16 vector lanes、128KiB SHM、4 HBM通道、无 cache |
| `project/compiler.py` | **可编辑的汇编生成器**（约600行 Python），`python -m project.compiler` 重新生成两个 .asm |
| `codesign/challenge/` | 冻结的评测器：ISA解析、FP32功能模拟（micro.py）、资源调度计时（pipeline_events.py/service.py）、面积功耗模型 |
| `programs/*.asm` | 生成的基线程序（P1 1843行，D1 2618行） |
| `baseline_manifest.json` | 冻结基线周期数，供 `grade` 对比 |
| `ABI.md` | 两个 case 的 HBM 符号表（FP32 元素偏移，非字节） |

## ISA 要点

每行 `OPCODE {json}`。核心：`WG.BEGIN/END`（指定 SM，每SM最多4个常驻workgroup）、`LD/ST`（HBM↔RF↔SH 搬运）、`MMA.ACC`（m×k @ k×n 累加，需TC>0）、`VEC`（add/sub/mul/div/fma/gt/select/max）、`REDUCE`（sum/max）、`SFU`（exp/rsqrt/tanh）、`WAIT/BARRIER`、`STEP.COMMIT`、静态 `FOR` 循环（编译期展开，支持仿射/min/mod 等表达式）。

## 基线程序的结构（也是主要优化空间）

`compiler.py` 里 `Builder` 提供 `gemm / layernorm / attention / attention_decode / add_rows / add_bias / gelu` 七个构件。基线非常朴素：

- **只用 1 个 workgroup `g` 放在 SM0**，8个SM闲置7个——最大的改进机会是跨 SM 并行（P1 的 batch=2、8个头、N维分块都是天然并行维度）。
- GEMM 分块固定 **8行×16列×48深**；中间结果全部往返 HBM scratch，没有 RF/SHM 驻留融合。
- attention 用完整的 store-score→reload→softmax→store-prob→reload 流程；可用在线 softmax 或 RF 内融合省掉 HBM 往返。
- RF 只用 lane 0–3（基线硬件 16 lanes × 1024 words/lane）。
- `shared_kib=128` 配了但 `shared_bytes=0` 没用；`dma_depth=1`、`dma_engines=1`，无 prefetch 流水。
- `Builder.gemm` 只支持 N tile ∈ {8,16} 且整除宽度——可以自己扩展尾部 tile 或更激进的切法。

## 迭代流程

```sh
python -m project.compiler                                   # 重新生成 asm
python challenge.py check    --hardware hardware.json --program-p1 programs/M1_P1.asm --program-d1 programs/M2_D1.asm --seed 7 --report check-1.json
python challenge.py estimate ... --report estimate-1.json    # 只看性能不验证正确性
python challenge.py grade    ... --baseline baseline_manifest.json --report grade-1.json
```

注意一个环境问题：本机是 **Python 3.14.3 且没装 numpy**，而作业要求 **Python 3.12.13 + NumPy 2.5.3** 做基线对比——真要跑 check/grade 之前需要先配环境（`baseline_manifest.json` 校验会核对 python/numpy 版本，版本不匹配 `grade` 会拒绝加载基线，但 `check`/`estimate` 应该仍能跑，只是需要 numpy）。

另外作业要求提交 `project/iteration-log.md` 和 `agent-trace/`（本次会话的 trace），目前 `project/` 下还没有这两个。

README 原文是 "the complete trace of **the agent sessions** used for this project"——复数、按"用过"界定，而不是按"哪个工具"界定。所以：

- **Devin 的 session + Codex 的 session 都要**，各自按原生格式导出即可（Devin transcript JSON / `--export` 的 ATIF；Codex 的 session JSONL）。工具不同没关系，混着放 `agent-trace/` 下，可以按工具或日期分子目录。
- **界定标准是"是否用于本项目"**：读 repo、改 compiler、跑实验、讨论设计决策的都算；与此作业无关的闲聊/别的项目不用交。

- 不用交的是：**别人的** trace（作业明确禁止研究/复用他人提交和 agent 轨迹）。

# Agent Briefing: Transformer Hardware–Program Co-design

Read this file first. It formulates the whole assignment for an incoming agent
session: what the problem is, what the rules are, how to iterate, and what must
be logged. Authoritative sources: `README.md` (statement), `ISA.md` (instruction
set), `ABI.md` (HBM layout), `ASSEMBLY_GUIDE.md` (program walkthrough), and the
frozen evaluator under `codesign/challenge/`.

## 1. The problem in one paragraph

This is a **joint hardware/software optimization** task for a teaching
accelerator. You must submit **one** accelerator configuration
(`hardware.json`) that runs **two** fixed assembly programs: a prompt-prefill
program (`programs/M1_P1.asm`) and an autoregressive-decode program
(`programs/M2_D1.asm`). A deterministic simulator scores correctness, cycle
count, chip area, and power. You may change hardware menu choices *and* freely
redesign the programs (tiling, fusion, workgroup placement, scheduling, data
movement). The submission unit is the triple
`(H, P_prefill, P_decode)`.

## 2. Objective and constraints

Simulated clock: **500 MHz**. Frozen baseline cycles:

- `M1_P1` (prefill): **30,996,995** cycles
- `M2_D1` (decode): **1,302,032** cycles

```
score = 1000 * sqrt( (30996995 / T_P1) * (1302032 / T_D1) )
```

Baseline scores 1000; there is no maximum. A submission is **eligible** only if:

- both programs are functionally correct
  (`abs(cand - ref) <= 1e-3 + 1e-3 * abs(ref)` on every required hidden/KV
  element; nonfinite values fail);
- chip area ≤ **24 mm²** (`Hardware.area_mm2()` in
  `codesign/challenge/hardware.py`, coefficients in `cost_v04.json`);
- each case's max rolling 1000-cycle average power ≤ **20 W**;
- each case's cycles ≤ 2× its own baseline.

## 3. The workload (fixed, not chosen)

FP32 decoder-only Transformer inference. Per layer:
`LN1 → QKV projection → causal attention (scale 1/sqrt(32)) → output proj +
residual → LN2 → w1+b1 → tanh-approx GELU → w2+b2 → residual`.
LayerNorm ε = 1e-5. No embedding, vocab head, sampling, or quantization.

| Case | Model | Scenario contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `M1_P1` | M1: 3 layers, width 256, 8 heads × 32, FFN 1024 (~2.37M params) | Batch 2 × 64-position prompts. Compute both prompts' hidden + per-layer K/V, then `STEP.COMMIT {"step":0}`, then compute the first new position for each batch element (attends to own prompt + itself). |
| `M2_D1` | M2: 2 layers, width 128, 4 heads × 32, FFN 512 (~0.40M params) | Batch 1, 128-position KV history already in HBM. Eight sequential decode steps; step `s` attends to 128 history + `s+1` generated positions; `STEP.COMMIT {"step":s}` for every `s=0..7` (later inputs release only after earlier commits). |

Inputs are teacher-forced hidden states — you do not pick tokens. Every
required output element must be written **exactly once** to its published ABI
region (`ABI.md`); weights/history are read-only; future inputs are unreadable
until released.

## 4. The machine and the hardware menu

GPU-inspired single chip: identical SMs (tensor-core-like `MMA.ACC` units,
vector lanes, SFUs, optional reduction units, a fixed 256 KiB RF per SM split
into private 64 KiB workgroup slots, optional shared memory, DMA engines),
a shared NoC, HBM channels, and an optional chip-wide cache. See the full menu
in `README.md` §2 — tunables include `sm_count`, `tc_count`/`tc_array`/
`tc_k_parallel`, `vector_lanes`, `sfu_lanes`, `reduction_units`, `rf_ports`,
`shared_kib`/`shared_banks`/`shared_ports`, `dma_depth`/`dma_engines`,
`sm_noc_bytes_per_cycle`, `multicast`, `noc_bytes_per_cycle`, `hbm_channels`,
`cache_mib`.

The timing model is a **deterministic resource scheduler**, not a GPU. Intuitions
from real GPUs are hypotheses to test, not rules. One hardware JSON serves both
cases.

## 5. ISA essentials (see `ISA.md` for the contract)

One `OPCODE {json}` per line. Opcodes: `WG.BEGIN`/`WG.END` (named workgroup on an
explicit SM; ≤4 resident per SM), `LD`/`ST` (HBM↔RF↔SH copies with optional
`shape`/`strides` tiles), `MMA.ACC` (`acc += a@b` on RF tiles, needs `tc_count>0`),
`VEC` (add/sub/mul/div/fma/gt/select/max), `REDUCE` (sum/max → 1 element),
`SFU` (exp/rsqrt/tanh), `WAIT`, `BARRIER`, `STEP.COMMIT`, static `FOR`/`END.FOR`
with compile-time integer expressions. Memory addresses are **FP32 element
offsets**, not bytes. Key traps: initialize RF/accumulators before reading;
events must be unique after loop expansion; cross-workgroup HBM ordering needs
explicit `WAIT`/`BARRIER`/commit; an `ST` may still be reading its RF/SH source
after issue.

## 6. The iteration loop (how an agent should work)

The assembly files are **generated**, not hand-edited. Edit
`project/compiler.py` (a small Python emitter with `Builder`, `gemm`,
`layernorm`, `attention`, `attention_decode`, helpers) or write your own
generator, then regenerate.

Environment: **`grade` refuses to run unless the interpreter is Python 3.12.13
with NumPy 2.5.3** — the frozen baseline manifest pins them. `check`/`estimate`
need NumPy installed. Set up such an env first (e.g. pyenv/uv).

```sh
python -m project.compiler                     # regenerate programs/*.asm
python challenge.py check    --hardware hardware.json \
    --program-p1 programs/M1_P1.asm --program-d1 programs/M2_D1.asm \
    --seed 7 --report project/check-N.json     # correctness FIRST
python challenge.py estimate ... --report project/estimate-N.json  # timing only
python challenge.py grade    ... --baseline baseline_manifest.json \
    --report project/grade-N.json              # public experimental score
```

Discipline: change **one idea at a time**; keep one `hardware.json` valid for
both programs; `estimate` is the fast exploration loop but only `check`
establishes correctness; keep every report file under `project/` as evidence.

## 7. Mandatory experiment log

After **every** experiment (a hardware or program change you evaluate), append
to `project/iteration-log.md` — this file is a **required submission artifact**
and proves the result was reached by genuine iteration. Entry template:

```markdown
## YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM — <one-line title>
- Change: <what changed, e.g. hardware.json field a→b, compiler tile 8→16>
- Verify: <command> -> <report path> -> passed/failed (+ why)
- Result: P1=… D1=… cycles (baseline 30996995/1302032), score ~…, area/power …
- Decision: keep/revert; next step and why
```

Also record rejected ideas — they are part of the evidence. Do not wait until
submission day; log as you go.

## 8. Frozen files — do not modify

`codesign/` (the evaluator), `MANIFEST.json`, `baseline_manifest.json`, and the
generated `programs/*.asm` (edit the *generator* instead). The grader executes
only the emitted assembly — never rely on Python scripts at grading time.

## 9. Submission packaging

ZIP (≤25 MiB) with these paths **at its root**:

```
hardware.json
programs/M1_P1.asm
programs/M2_D1.asm
project/iteration-log.md
project/<generator sources, scripts, experiment reports>
agent-trace/<all agent session exports, native format, ≥1 nonempty>
```

`agent-trace/` must contain the traces of **every agent session used on this
project, across all tools** (e.g. Devin transcripts from
`~/.local/share/devin/cli/transcripts/*.json` or `devin --export` ATIF files;
Codex session JSONL). Include dead ends. Deadlines: milestone 1 = **2026-10-07
12:00 Beijing**; milestone 2 (final) = **2026-10-12 12:00 Beijing**.

## 10. Repo map and current state

| Path | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `hardware.json` | Current shared accelerator config (baseline: 8 SM, 2×4x8 TC, 16 vec lanes, 128 KiB SHM, 4 HBM ch, no cache) |
| `project/compiler.py` | Editable program generator — the main thing you change |
| `programs/*.asm` | Generated output; regenerate, don't hand-edit |
| `codesign/challenge/` | Frozen parser/executor/scheduler/cost model — read-only |
| `baseline_manifest.json` | Frozen baseline metrics for `grade` |
| `ABI.md` | Every HBM symbol, offset, shape, release step |
| `ASSEMBLY_GUIDE.md` | Map of the generated programs' block structure |

Git: branch `dev-yh`, remote `origin` = GitHub `YihDu/SLAI-infra-course-hw1`.
Status at briefing time: unmodified baseline committed; no experiments run yet.

## 11. Known baseline weaknesses → first hypotheses to test

The shipped baseline is deliberately naive; all of these are *measured* targets:

1. **One workgroup on SM 0** — 7 of 8 SMs idle. P1's batch=2, per-head, and
   N-column parallelism are free concurrency; D1 is sequential across steps but
   parallel across heads/layers' weights prefetch.
2. **All intermediates round-trip HBM scratch** — fuse LN→QKV, attention, and
   FFN stages in RF/SHM where capacity allows.
3. **Fixed 8×16×48 GEMM tiles, N-tile restricted to 8/16** — larger/other tiles,
   tail tiles, and better K splits may raise TC utilization.
4. **Attention materializes scores/probs in HBM** — online softmax or RF-resident
   attention removes traffic.
5. **`shared_kib=128` paid for but `shared_bytes=0`** — unused area; either use
   SHM for staged weights/KV or drop it to save area.
6. **No DMA pipelining** (`dma_depth=1`, 1 engine) and no cache — prefetch and
   `cache_mib`/`multicast` may hide HBM latency.

Measure each against the simulator; keep what measurably helps on **both** cases.

arguments.content:
# Problem Formulation: Transformer Hardware–Program Co-design

This document abstracts the assignment into a self-contained optimization
problem. It is written so that any agent (or reader) can understand *what* is
being optimized, *over which space*, *under which oracle*, and *why* the
solution method is an agent-guided search loop — without first reading the
whole starter package.

## 1. Decision variables

The artifact to produce is a triple:

```
(H, P_prefill, P_decode)
```

- **H** — one accelerator configuration drawn from a fixed hardware menu
  (~120.7 billion raw combinations). Each SM may carry matrix engines (TCs),
  vector lanes, SFUs, reduction units, a fixed 256 KiB register file, optional
  shared memory, and DMA engines; chip-wide choices are the NoC bandwidth,
  per-SM NoC links, HBM channel count, multicast, and an optional shared cache.
  H is described by `hardware.json` and is **shared by both programs**.

- **P_prefill** — an assembly program for case `M1_P1`: batch 2 × 64-position
  prompt prefill through model M1 (3 layers, width 256, 8×32 heads, FFN 1024),
  then one new position per batch element.

- **P_decode** — an assembly program for case `M2_D1`: eight sequential decode
  steps through model M2 (2 layers, width 128, 4×32 heads, FFN 512) against a
  128-position KV history.

The program space is open-ended: tiling and tail tiles, loop order, RF/shared
memory residency, fusion, recomputation, attention algorithm (e.g. online
softmax), workgroup count and SM placement, DMA scheduling, synchronization.
Programs are emitted by an editable generator (`project/compiler.py`), not
hand-written.

## 2. The computation (fixed workload)

Both cases run the same layer function, in FP32:

```
x ──> LN1 ──> QKV proj ──> causal attention (scale 1/√32) ──> WO proj ──> +x ──>
    ──> LN2 ──> W1+b1 ──> tanh-GELU ──> W2+b2 ──> +residual ──> x'
```

Per layer, newly computed K/V must be exported to the ABI regions. Final-layer
hidden states go to `output/hidden`. LayerNorm ε = 1e-5. There is no
embedding, vocab projection, sampling, or quantization.

The interface contract that makes the two cases different:

- **P1**: must write *both* prompts' outputs and K/V, then
  `STEP.COMMIT {"step":0}` releases the two `input/step0` vectors; the two
  first-new-position results are checked at case end.
- **D1**: `input/step{s}` is readable only after steps `< s` commit; every step
  `s=0..7` must produce output+K/V then `STEP.COMMIT {"step":s}`. Attention at
  step `s` covers 128 history + `s+1` generated positions.

## 3. Objective function

Deterministic simulated execution at a fixed 500 MHz clock. Frozen baseline
cycle counts: `T_P1^0 = 30,996,995`, `T_D1^0 = 1,302,032`.

```
score(H, P1, P2) = 1000 · sqrt( T_P1^0 / T_P1  ·  T_D1^0 / T_D1 )   if eligible
                 = ineligible → no score                          otherwise
```

The geometric mean weights both cases equally in log-space: a 2× speedup on
one case is worth the same as √2× on both.

## 4. Constraints (eligibility gates)

1. **Correctness** — FP32 functional executor compares every required hidden
   and new-K/V element: `|cand − ref| ≤ 1e-3 + 1e-3·|ref|`; nonfinite fails.
   Instruction-level rules: initialize before read, write required outputs
   exactly once, never read unreleased inputs, unique events, legal RF/SH/HBM
   views, all workgroups ended, commits in order.
2. **Area** — `area(H) ≤ 24 mm²`, per the formula in `hardware.py` with
   coefficients `cost_v04.json`.
3. **Power** — per case, max rolling 1000-cycle average ≤ 20 W.
4. **Latency floor** — each case ≤ 2× its own baseline cycles.

## 5. The oracle

`challenge.py` provides three evaluation modes over `(hardware.json, asm,
asm)`:

- `estimate` — timing only (fast exploration signal; does not prove
  correctness);
- `check` — functional correctness against public seed inputs;
- `grade` — correctness + timing + gates → public experimental score.

Timing comes from a deterministic resource scheduler
(`pipeline_events.py`, `service.py`): instruction issue, TC/vector/SFU
service times, RF/SH port contention, DMA queues, NoC and HBM channel
contention, cache behavior. **This model — not GPU intuition — is ground
truth.** Properties that matter on real GPUs may not hold here and vice versa.

## 6. Why this is a co-design problem

H and P interact: more TCs only pay off if the program emits tiles that fill
them; more SMs only help if workgroups are placed on them; shared memory/cache
only pay if the schedule creates reuse; area spent on unused resources is pure
cost. The space is far too large for enumeration (~1.2×10¹¹ hardware configs
× effectively unbounded program space), and the objective is only measurable
through the simulator — so this is a **black-box, constrained optimization /
program-synthesis** problem.

## 7. The agentic solution method

The intended method is an explicit search loop driven by an AI agent, with
measured feedback:

```
repeat:
    1. PROPOSE  — pick a joint change (H field(s) and/or generator change),
                  informed by the accumulated experiment history
    2. GENERATE — run the compiler to emit both .asm programs
    3. VERIFY   — `check` must pass; reject on any correctness violation
    4. MEASURE  — `estimate`/`grade` → cycles, area, power, score
    5. LEARN    — record the outcome in project/iteration-log.md;
                  keep, revert, or branch the search
until diminishing returns or deadline
```

Design rules for the search: one idea per iteration; `estimate` for cheap
screening, `check` before trusting any candidate; keep `hardware.json` legal
for both programs; never hand-edit `.asm` (edit the generator); never modify
the frozen evaluator (`codesign/`, `baseline_manifest.json`).

Optional aids are allowed but not required: MILP for bounded subproblems,
heuristic cost models, compiler passes — the judge only scores the emitted
hardware+assembly.

## 8. Process constraints (part of the deliverable)

Because submissions are graded partly on demonstrated process:

- every evaluated candidate → an entry in `project/iteration-log.md`;
- every agent session used on the project → its native trace file under
  `agent-trace/` (all tools, all sessions, including dead ends);
- generator sources and experiment reports stay under `project/`.

Final ZIP (root paths): `hardware.json`, `programs/M1_P1.asm`,
`programs/M2_D1.asm`, `project/…`, `agent-trace/…`.
Deadlines (Beijing): milestone 1 = 2026-10-07 12:00; final = 2026-10-12 12:00.

## 9. Environment prerequisite

`grade` validates that the runtime matches the frozen baseline's pinned
environment: **Python 3.12.13 + NumPy 2.5.3** (`cli.py` `_load_baseline`
compares them). `check`/`estimate` need NumPy. Set up that interpreter before
the first experiment.
